files.text: --- title: "Ask for smooth motion and transitions" sidebarTitle: "Motion and transitions" description: "The words that change how a HyperFrames video moves: fix motion you don't like, ask for camera, overlap, depth and pace, and pick transitions between scenes." --- import { DocsVideo } from "/snippets/docs-video.jsx"; Your agent already follows HyperFrames' motion rules: elements land and hold still, moves overlap, cuts happen mid-motion. Use this page when you want to steer it: what to say when the motion feels wrong, and the ideas worth asking for by name. ## Fix motion you don't like Watch the video once, then tell your agent what you see in plain words. These phrasings work: | What you see | Say | What the agent changes | | --- | --- | --- | | Everything moves too fast | "Too fast. Slow the zooms and pans." | Slows every camera move to about 0.7× and leaves the rest alone | | It drags | "Speed this up." | Shortens each beat along with its content, and moves later beats earlier | | Titles keep floating or growing after they appear | "Land the titles, then hold them still." | Titles arrive, stop dead, and leave with the scene | | It feels like slides | "It feels like slides. Carry one thing across each cut." | Enters the next scene through something on screen and cuts mid-move | | Everything appears at once | "Bring things in one after another, on the voice." | Staggers entrances so each starts before the last has settled | | It looks bouncy or cheap | "No bounce on text or UI." | Uses long, smooth slow-downs; keeps overshoot for physical objects | | There's a jump at a cut | "There's a jump at 4.2 s." | Matches positions and speeds on both sides of that cut | | A scene sits there with nothing happening | "Scene 3 is dead. Give it something to do." | Adds real action: the UI working, footage, the camera travelling to the next thing | Give a timestamp when you can ("at 4.2 s"). Ask for one change at a time and watch again. Free 16-minute lesson with a short video, a quiz and a brief to try. A beat is a change on screen with a time: a word appears, a card leaves, a cut lands. ## Ideas worth asking for Each idea below has a side-by-side film: the same scene built twice, where the only difference is one line of the prompt. Left is without, right is with. ### Move only what is live Once something lands, it holds still. What keeps moving is what is actually changing: a live number, a feed, a progress bar. Don't ask for "subtle breathing" to make a scene feel alive; it reads as generated. > The panel lands by 1.9 s. After that, only what the feed changes moves: a reading arrives every 300 ms, the last digits change, the sparkline extends one segment, `LAST SYNC` restamps. Nothing else moves. *Left: the whole panel freezes at 2 s, so it looks like a dead connection. Right: only the readings move, and the rest is still.* ### Move the camera to get somewhere A camera move earns its place by travelling between things, so the viewer sees they live in one space. A slow creeping push-in for its own sake does not. > Lay the five pipeline stages out 640 px apart, wider than the frame, and move the camera across the whole run. A packet runs the wire and lights each stage as it arrives. *Left: five stages cross-fade in one spot. Right: you travel to each one, and the neighbours stay in view.* ### Overlap, don't queue The next element starts while the last is still settling. Stagger things that happen in sequence. Things that already existed show up together. > The rollout spreads outward from `us-east-1`, reaching each region 0.09 s apart in order of distance. Each region's 0.5 s ignite is still running when the next three begin. *Left: twelve regions light on one frame, so you can't tell where it started. Right: it visibly spreads.* ### One idea per move Combine properties only when they say the same thing. Rising and fading in says "arriving". Adding a spin and a zoom makes text unreadable mid-flight. > The confirmation sheet rises 470 px over 1.2 s while fading in. Rotation, scale and blur are never touched. *Same travel and timing. Left: "Payment confirmed" is a tilted smear. Right: readable the whole way up.* ### Weight for physical objects only Overshoot says "this has mass". Use it on things that have weight, like flaps, cards and characters. Never use it on text, UI or numbers: a counter that flies past 42 and falls back shows a number that was never true. > The split-flap plates swing past their rest position and settle; the housing recoils when they land. The gate number never overshoots 42. ### Depth: near things move faster Far layers move slower than the camera and near ones faster. One blurred foreground object passing in front of the content is the strongest depth cue. A second one is clutter. > The horizon row moves at a fifth of the room's rate, the racks at full rate, and one near column sweeps past at six times, blurred, crossing in front of the headline. ### Pace to the format A showreel gives each idea 1–4 seconds; a product demo holds one framing for 7–10 seconds while the UI works. Stretching a 2-second idea to 8 seconds feels slow however well it moves. > Showreel pace: 1.1 s per beat, cutting hard, all three beats delivered by 3.3 s. ## Handmade, still deterministic For a stop-motion or hand-animated feel, ask for movement that steps between held positions, with the irregularity coming from a seed. Every render must give the same frame at the same time, so unseeded randomness is not allowed. > Paper-cutout shapes on visible wires, like stop-motion. Seed a random offset per element (same seed every render) and hold each position for exactly two frames, quantized on the frame index. *Rendered from the prompt above, unedited. Two renders came back byte-identical.* Say "two frames", not "0.067 seconds": a hold measured in seconds drifts into uneven one- and three-frame steps. ## Between scenes: transitions A good transition is caused by something on screen: the camera zooms through a button into the next screen, a card grows until it becomes the next scene, the background floods a new colour while the subject stays. Ask for that kind of handoff and the agent builds it. Use 3–5 kinds in a film, each where it fits, and never a dissolve between two unrelated scenes. To pin a specific effect, name a block from the catalog and the seam it goes on: > Six-scene SaaS explainer. Use [`whip-pan`](/catalog/blocks/whip-pan) between related points, and one [`cinematic-zoom`](/catalog/blocks/cinematic-zoom) into the final pricing reveal. About 0.4 s each. *Rendered from the prompt above, unedited.* | Energy | Shader blocks | CSS blocks | Duration | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Calm (wellness, brand story) | [`cross-warp-morph`](/catalog/blocks/cross-warp-morph), [`light-leak`](/catalog/blocks/light-leak) | [`transitions-blur`](/catalog/blocks/transitions-blur) | 0.5–0.8 s | | Medium (SaaS, explainer) | [`whip-pan`](/catalog/blocks/whip-pan), [`cinematic-zoom`](/catalog/blocks/cinematic-zoom) | [`transitions-push`](/catalog/blocks/transitions-push), [`transitions-cover`](/catalog/blocks/transitions-cover) | 0.3–0.5 s | | High (promo, music, launch) | [`ridged-burn`](/catalog/blocks/ridged-burn), [`glitch`](/catalog/blocks/glitch), [`chromatic-radial-split`](/catalog/blocks/chromatic-radial-split) | [`transitions-scale`](/catalog/blocks/transitions-scale), [`transitions-light`](/catalog/blocks/transitions-light) | 0.15–0.3 s | Shader blocks warp and morph both scenes pixel by pixel; use them when the handoff itself is a moment. CSS blocks are lighter and fit ordinary scene changes. All of them are in the [catalog](/catalog/blocks/cross-warp-morph); a name that isn't there (`page-curl`) leaves the agent guessing. **Don't ask to fade one scene out and then fade the next one in.** It renders as a jump cut with a dip in the middle. The transition is the exit: ask for "`cross-warp-morph` from scene 1 to scene 2". Free 16-minute lesson with a short video, a quiz and a brief to try. Name the cut: a hard cut is an instant switch, a match cut carries a move across it, a zoom cut pushes in and pulls back. ## Related - [Plan scenes with a storyboard](/prompting/design-systems#storyboards) - [Add voice, music and sound](/prompting/media-and-audio) - [A complete film, from prompt to render](/prompting/capstone) ## Words for how motion feels Describe how motion should *feel* and the agent picks the matching GSAP ease: | Say this | Agent uses | Feels like | | ----------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------ | | smooth | `power2.out` | Natural deceleration | | snappy | `power4.out` | Quick and decisive | | bouncy | `back.out` | Overshoots then settles | | springy | `elastic.out` | Oscillates into place | | dramatic | `expo.out` | Fast start, long glide | | dreamy | `sine.inOut` | Slow, symmetrical | **Timing shorthand:** fast (0.2s) = energy, medium (0.4s) = professional, slow (0.6s) = luxury, very slow (1–2s) = cinematic.
